text: What does `adder(int n) { return x -> x + n; }` actually produce?
choices: A partially applied static method, resolved by the JIT at the first call.
A new anonymous class per distinct value of `n`, generated at run time.
A reference into `adder`'s stack frame, kept alive by the returned lambda.
An object holding the captured value and code that uses it — a closure, which is also a one-field, one-method object.
explanation: `n` lived in `adder`'s stack frame, which was destroyed when `adder` returned, and the lambda still has it because the value was copied in. `adder(5).apply(1)` gives 6 and `adder(100).apply(1)` gives 101 — two functions from one method. That a closure and a one-field object are the same thing under two notations is the Lambda Papers' claim, visible in six lines.
